title: Indian Founders and CEOs to Help Train US Manufacturing Workers Under New Federal Program
excerpt: The Trump administration's Foundry School, a Stanford-led initiative, will tap enterprise leaders from India and other Pax Silica partner nations to teach advanced manufacturing skills to American workers.
body:
• The Trump administration launched Foundry School on September 3, a Stanford-led workforce program to train advanced manufacturing workers across eight US university campuses.
  • Enterprise founders and CEOs from India, Japan, South Korea, and Taiwan will deliver instruction alongside American industry leaders as part of the Pax Silica framework.
  • Federal projections estimate the US will need 3.8 million skilled manufacturing workers by 2033 across semiconductors, defence, and energy sectors.
  • India's inclusion reflects the deepening US-India technology partnership, with prior bilateral discussions on semiconductor manufacturing, AI adoption, and critical minerals.

The Trump administration launched Foundry School on September 3, a national workforce program that will draw on enterprise founders and chief executives from India and four other nations to train American workers for a manufacturing sector the government says will need 3.8 million skilled employees by 2033.

Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio headlined the launch at the Donald J. Trump Institute of Peace in Washington. Under Secretary of State for Economic Affairs Jacob Helberg, who first announced the program at the Pax Silica summit in June, hosted the event alongside university presidents and manufacturing executives.

How the Program Works

Foundry School operates through an academic-workforce partnership anchored by Stanford University. Stanford developed a first-of-its-kind advanced manufacturing curriculum incorporating instruction from seven partner institutions: Arizona State University, Georgia Tech, Ohio State University, Penn State, the University of Cincinnati, the University of Kansas, and Vanderbilt University.

https://x.com/suraj_sharma14/status/2096637047452893335

The curriculum runs across 17 sessions at the eight campuses, taught directly by founders and CEOs from advanced manufacturing enterprises in the United States and Pax Silica partner economies — India, Japan, South Korea, and Taiwan.

The program unfolds in two phases. Seven regional sessions beginning in September 2026 cover factory design, materials and supply chains, assembly-line engineering, plant economics, regulation, and workforce development. A 10-session core program at Stanford starting in January 2027 tackles precision tooling, industrial automation, quality systems, digital manufacturing, and defence production.

India's Role in the Framework

India's inclusion as a Pax Silica partner nation means Indian manufacturing leaders will teach alongside their American, Japanese, Korean, and Taiwanese counterparts. The State Department described the initiative as a course designed to ensure the American workforce benefits from 'America's industrial renaissance.'

The arrangement builds on bilateral technology cooperation that has accelerated in recent months. In June, India's Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology Secretary S. Krishnan met with Helberg to discuss collaboration in semiconductor manufacturing, AI adoption, and securing access to critical minerals.

"This is about universities and industry working together to accelerate all things associated with enhancing workforce preparation, enhancement and competitiveness."

— Michael Crow, ASU President

Indian companies have been expanding their US manufacturing footprint in parallel. At the SelectUSA Investment Summit earlier this year, twelve Indian companies collectively pledged over $1 billion in new capital commitments across aerospace, defence, energy, and advanced manufacturing, with projected creation of approximately 1,500 US positions.

The Workforce Gap

Federal projections indicate domestic industrial operations will require an estimated 3.8 million skilled workers by 2033 across semiconductors, defence, energy, and related sectors. The State Department framed Foundry School as a bridge between the capital flowing into new factories and the workforce needed to operate them.

The reindustrialization push has brought substantial private investment commitments into the United States, but labour shortages in advanced manufacturing remain a persistent challenge. The program aims to address that gap through direct instruction from industry practitioners rather than traditional academic coursework alone.

Pax Silica Context

Foundry School is a component of Pax Silica, the State Department's flagship multilateral effort to secure trusted global supply chains for critical technologies. The framework also includes PaxPass, a platform announced at the June summit to streamline the movement of AI-related goods through cargo verification and AI-powered risk assessment, backed by $50 million in US foreign assistance funding.

For the Indian diaspora, the program represents a notable shift: Indian industrial expertise is being formally incorporated into the architecture of American economic competitiveness, moving beyond the traditional narrative of Indian talent filling individual corporate roles.
